However, no axis-parallel partition exists with this property. If it existed, it would correspond to partitioning the values of C and F into light and heavy, but then the first join derived from (22) joins the light-C with heavy-F , while the second joins the heavy-C with the light-F , which leaves out the combinations light-light and heavy-heavy. Conclusion The PANDAExpress algorithm has two key aspects. The first is the idea of leveraging information theoretic inequalities to derive high-level query plans; and the second is to collect precise skewness information during the execution of the query plan in order to partition the data based on general hyperplane cuts to avoid skews. The partitioning strategies are designed to load-balance the computation among all sub-query plans. Since we were interested in meeting the worst-case bounds defined by the submodular width, we used the threshold parameter B to guide the partitioning of the data. We believe that this idea of load-balancing data processing amongst different sub-query plans is a powerful and practical idea. An interesting future direction to explore is to see if the load-balancing can be more adaptive to the actual data distribution. The key remaining open question at the center of the PANDA framework is to bound the length of the proof sequence needed to prove a given Shannon-flow inequality. Let (Z, D) be parameters of the integral Shannon-flow inequality (4) witnessed by (M, S). We start with i = 0: (D0 , M0 , S0 ) := (D, M, S), and we will iteratively construct (Di+1 , Mi+1 , Si+1 ). By Proposition 2.2, identity (5) holds. If Z ⊆ Di (in the multiset sense), then we are done; no proof step is needed. So let’s assume Z ̸⊆ Di . We first claim that there must be at least one unconditional term W ∈ Di that is not in Z. Assume for the sake of contradiction that there is no unconditional term in Di . Set all (symbolic) variables h(X) := 1, X ̸= ∅. Then, h(Y |X) is 0 if X ̸= ∅, and 1 otherwise. Moreover, h(Y |X) ≥ 0 and h(Y ; Z|X) ≥ 0. Hence, the LHS of (5) is exactly |Z| and the RHS is at most the number of unconditional terms in Di . Therefore, the number of unconditional terms in Di must be at least |Z|. If every unconditional term in Di is also in Z, then Z must be the set of unconditional terms in Di . This contradicts our assumption that Z ̸⊆ Di . Next, take any W ∈ Di that is not in Z. Since identity (5) holds, there must be some term that cancels h(W ). We consider a few cases: • If (Y |W ) ∈ Di so that h(Y |W ) cancels h(W ), then we define Di+1 := Di \ {W , (Y |W )} ∪ {Y W }, Mi+1 := Mi Si+1 := Si and add to the proof sequence the composition step h(W ) + h(Y |W ) → h(Y W ). • If (Y |X) ∈ Mi where W = Y X so that −h(Y |X) cancels h(W ), then we define Di+1 := Di \ {W } ∪ {X}, Mi+1 := Mi \ {(Y |X)}, Si+1 := Si and add to the proof sequence the monotonicity step h(W ) → h(X). • If (Y ; Z|X) ∈ Si so that −h(Y ; Z|X) cancels h(W ), where W = XY , then we define Di+1 := Di \ {W } ∪ {(X), (Y |XZ)}, Mi+1 := Mi , Si+1 := Si \ {(Y ; Z|X)} and add to the proof sequence two steps: the first is a decomposition step h(W ) → h(X) + h(Y |X), and the second is a submodularity step h(Y |X) → h(Y |XZ). In all cases above, the potential function |D| + |M| + 3|S| decreases by at least 1 per every step added. □
